articles.title: Active Sessions
articles.content:
# Active Sessions

## Overview

- Active Sessions displays the users who are currently logged in to ViciECM applications.
- Administrators can view the logged-in user's details, identify which application they are accessing and check when they logged in.
- Administrators can also terminate individual sessions or close all active sessions at once.

## Session Details

The Active Sessions grid displays the following information:

- **Full Name:** Displays the name of the logged-in user along with their username.
- **Application Name:** Displays the name of the application the user is currently accessing.
- **Logged In Date/Time:** Displays the date and time when the user logged in.

## Session Management

### Close Session

- Click the **Close Session** icon against the required user to terminate their active session.
- This allows administrators to end an individual user's session without affecting other logged-in users.

### Close All

- Click **Close All** to terminate the active sessions of all logged-in users.
- This option is useful when administrators need to end all active sessions at once.

### Refresh

- Click **Refresh** to reload the Active Sessions grid.
- This displays the latest available session information.

> **Note:** The Generated Time displayed above the grid indicates when the session information was generated.

articles.title: External Users
articles.content:
# External Users

## Purpose

The **External Users** section in ViciECM allows administrators to manage existing external user access by updating the expiry time and viewing the assigned access level.

## Features

### 1. View External Username
Displays the existing external username. This field is read-only and cannot be modified.

### 2. Update Expiry Time
Allows administrators to modify the expiry date and time. This is a mandatory field.

### 3. View Access Level
Displays the assigned access level (**Read** or **Edit**). The access level cannot be modified from this section.

### 4. View External User Details
Displays information such as the username, mode, logical path, job name, workflow name, and expiry time.

### 5. Edit External User Settings
Allows administrators to modify the expiry time using the Edit (pencil) icon corresponding to an existing entry.

## How to Update an External User

### Step 1: Navigate to External Users
Navigate to **Administration → External Users**.

### Step 2: Locate the External User
Locate the external user whose settings need to be updated.

### Step 3: Edit External User Details
Click the **Edit (pencil) icon** in the corresponding row.

### Step 4: View External Username
View the **External Username**. The username cannot be edited.

### Step 5: View Access Level
View the assigned **Access** level (Read or Edit). This field is displayed for reference only and cannot be changed.

### Step 6: Update Expiry Time
Enter or select the required **Expiry Time** using the date and time fields. This field is mandatory.

### Step 7: Save Changes
Click **Update** to save the changes.

### Step 8: Cancel Changes
Click **Cancel** to discard the changes.
## Access Levels

### 1. Read Level Access gives you the following permissions:

- Search
- View
- Print
- Download

### 2. Edit Level Access gives you the following permissions:

- Search
- View
- Print
- Download
- Modify Documents
- Add Annotations

articles.title: Group Management
articles.content:
# Group Management

## Overview

- Group Management is used to create and manage groups of users.
- Multiple users can be assigned to a single group.
- Users assigned to a group inherit the permissions configured for that group.
- Administrators can create groups, assign users, update group details and manage group status.

## Group Creation

1. Click **Add New Group** to create a new group.
2. Enter the Group Name and Description. Both fields are mandatory.
3. Click the **Add** icon to save the group.
4. The newly created group will appear in the Group Management grid.

## User Assignment

ViciECM provides three ways to assign users to groups.

### Method 1: Through Group Management

1. Navigate to **Administration → Groups**.
2. Click the **Add Users** icon against the required group.
3. The Select User(s) window displays the available active users.
4. Select the users you want to add to the group.
5. Click **Save** to apply the changes.

### Method 2: Through User Management

1. Navigate to **Administration → Users**.
2. Locate the required user in the Users grid.
3. Go to the **Action** column.
4. Click on **Add to Group** to add the selected user to the required group(s).

### Method 3: Through User Creation / Edit User Form

1. Navigate to **Administration → Users**.
2. Open the user creation form or select an existing user and click **Edit**.
3. Locate the **Groups** field in the form.
4. Select the required group(s) from the available list.
5. Click **Save** to apply the changes.

> **Note:** This is the only method that allows both Active and Inactive users to be assigned to groups.

### Select User(s) Window

The Select User(s) window opens when users are assigned through the Group Management page.

#### Fields

- **Type:** Displays the user icon.
- **Name:** Displays the name of the user.
- **Selected:** Indicates whether the user is selected for the group.

#### Options

- **Select All The Above User[s]:** Selects all users visible in the grid.

> **Note:** The Select User(s) window displays only active users. Selecting all users applies only to the users visible on the current page.

### User Selection Process

1. Click the **Add Users** icon against the required group.
2. Select the required users.
3. Click **Save** to apply the selection.
4. Click **Cancel** to close the window without saving the changes.

## Group Modification

- Click the **Update** icon to save changes made to the group details.
- Click **Cancel** to discard the modifications.

## Group Status Management

- Each group can have either Active or Inactive status.
- A green tick indicates that the group is Active.
- A grey tick indicates that the group is Inactive.
- Click the status icon to change the group's status.
- To inactivate multiple groups, select the required groups and click **Inactive Group(s)**.

## Export Operations

- **Export To Excel:** Exports group details to an Excel file.
- **Export To PDF:** Exports group details to a PDF file.
- The export dropdown provides two options:
  - **Current Page:** Exports the groups displayed on the current page.
  - **All Pages:** Exports all available group records.

articles.title: User Management
articles.content:
# User Management

## List of Functionalities

### Buttons 
- Add User
- Import User
- Swap User
- Inactive User
- Export to PDF / Excel with
  Current Page / All Pages Dropdown

### Actions
- Edit (Click on Edit)
- We will get 4 options - Update - Add to group - Profile Edit - Cancel.

## List of Columns in the Data Grid
- Photo
- Username
- First Name
- Last Name
- Mobile No.
- User Type
- User Pool
- Department
- Email ID
- Status
- Actions

## Add User (Just Click on the Button)

### Username (Mandatory Field)
- Once user is created, it cannot be changed.
- Min 1 Character is necessary.
- Max 50 Characters. 
- Accepts Alphabets, Numbers, and Alphanumeric characters.
- Cannot create Username Duplicates as it is Case - insensitive.

### Password / Change Password
- Once password is created, can be updated again.
- Password and Confirm Password has to match.
- It is Case - Sensitive.
- What kind of characters are accepted and how many characters depends on Pwd Rules Tab in the Configuration.

### First Name
- This is a Mandatory Field.
- Min 1
- Max 100
- All characters allowed except few Special Characters like $%<> , 

### Type of User (Mandatory)
- Administration: This user has much higher access then normal or Scanner user.

- Normal:  Can't access Admin Module
         - Can't access few Portlets in Dashboard Module like All Jobs, Backup Details, Volume Information, User Information, Logged in Users and Data Extraction.

 - Can't access few Sub - Modules in Manage like Purge Mails, Upload Logo, there is no "ALL USERS" Hyperlink in the recycle Bin. And also, no access to metadata import.

- A normal user cannot access Workflow - Designer but if he is added to a group called as 
"WFDESIGNERGROUP" that allows the normal user to access designer menu.

- Workflow - No Form Reports.

- Reports - No ECM.

- Workflow Reports - Normal - Cannot access User wise Job Details
- Workflow-wise job details only available for the Super-Admin.

- Scanner - Only used to Scan and upload the physical documents into the Repository.

- By Default, this type of user has no permission   for Cabinet Creation and Document type Creation.

### User Pool (Mandatory)

- Named User Pool: Licenses are assigned individually to users. To accommodate new users beyond the license limit, existing users must be removed to free up licenses.

- Concurrent User Pool: Total licenses = 25; total users = 50. Only 25 users can access the repository at a time on a first-come, first-served basis.

### Email ID (Mandatory)

### Cabinet Creation
- User cannot create new Cabinets without this permission.

### Doc Type Creation 
- User cannot create new Document Type without this permission.

### User Status
- Set to Active / Inactive.

### Add to group  
- Can add new / existing user / inactive user to any single / Multiple groups.

## Inactive User
- Using this, you can turn active users into Inactive users.
- You can turn single / multiple users into inactive users.

## Swap User
- Using this feature, We can transfer the ownership of the files from old user to new user.
- In this process, User Type will also get swapped.
- The New User will replace old user
- The files and folders the new user will have = new user + old user
- On the other hand, The old user becomes inactive.

## Export
- The Export dropdown provides two options for exporting the user list:
   1) Current Page: Exports the user list displayed on the current page.
   2) All Pages: Exports the complete user list across all pages.
- The user list can be exported in Excel or PDF format.

## Import Users
- Using this feature, we can download a sample Excel template (.xlsx) and upload a list of multiple users to create them in a single operation.
- We should ensure that all mandatory fields in the Excel sheet are populated. Non-mandatory fields can be left blank.
- We should not delete any existing columns from the Excel template, as doing so may cause the Import Users process to fail.

articles.title: 00_Overview
articles.content:
# Auto-Deployment

## Overview

Auto-Deployment is a process used to deploy software updates to a target server in a controlled and automated manner.

## Why Is Auto-Deployment Used?

The main purpose is to deploy a software update without manually performing every individual operation on the server.

## What Does the Auto-Deployment Process Involve?

- Preparing the deployment package
- Configuring the required Client and Version in VCDeploy
- Uploading the deployment package
- Configuring the target server
- Executing the deployment

## Deployment Phases

1. **Phase 1 – Deployment Package Preparation:** Prepare the required folders and deployment files on the local PC.
2. **Phase 2 – VCDeploy Configuration:** Create the Client and Client Version, upload the ZIP package, and verify deployment readiness.
3. **Phase 3 – Server Configuration and Execution:** Configure the target server and execute the deployment command.

articles.title: 01_Phase_1_Deployment_Package_Preparation
articles.content:
# Auto-Deployment – Phase 1

## Deployment Package Preparation

Begin the preparation process once the required patch folders have been received.

## 1. Receive the Required Patch Folders

Once the required patch folders are received, review the supplied patch package and identify the folders and files required for deployment.

## 2. Create a Date-Based Folder on the Local PC

Create a new folder on the local PC using the current date.

### Folder Naming Format

Use the following format:

`DD-MMM-YYYY`

Examples:

- `14-Sep-2026`
- `20-Oct-2026`

The month must be written using a three-letter abbreviation.

## 3. Create the Required Folders

Create the following four folders inside the date-based folder:

- `Server`
- `Register`
- `Testing`
- `Database`

## 3.1 Server Folder

The received patch contains a folder named `Server`.

Copy the required contents from the patch Server folder into the locally created Server folder.

### Important: Items to Exclude

Copy the required folders present in the Server folder, but do **not** copy the following items:

- `Flags`
- `ViciECMPatch`
- `ViciECMPatch.zip`

These files/folders must not be included in the deployment package.

## 3.2 Register Folder

The Register folder must contain the required batch files:

- `Register`
- `Unregister`

## 3.3 Testing Folder (Optional)

If Performance and/or Functionality testing is going to be performed, include the relevant folders inside the Testing folder.

Required subfolders, depending on the testing enabled:

- `Performance/`
- `Functionality/`

### Testing ZIP File Names

The ZIP files must be named exactly as specified in `config.json`:

- `Results_Performance.zip`
- `Results_Functionality.zip`

The Testing folder is optional. Include it only when performance or functionality testing is required.

## 3.4 Database Folder

The Database folder must contain the required SQL deployment and rollback scripts, if provided.

First, identify whether the repository is connected to:

- SQL Server
- Oracle Server

For each applicable database type, both Deploy and Rollback scripts are required. Take the required scripts from the Patch folder.

### SQL Server – Expected File Names

- `Sql_Rep_Deploy.sql`
- `Sql_Rep_Rollback.sql`
- `Sql_Rp_Deploy.sql`
- `Sql_Rp_Rollback.sql`

### Oracle – Expected File Names

- `Ora_Rep_Deploy.sql`
- `Ora_Rep_Rollback.sql`
- `Ora_Rp_Deploy.sql`
- `Ora_Rp_Rollback.sql`

## 4. Consolidating SQL Deployment Scripts

In the documented example, four `.txt` files containing SQL database deployment scripts were provided.

Follow these steps to consolidate the scripts into a single SQL deployment file:

1. Create a new blank text file on the local PC.
2. Copy and paste the contents of all four `.txt` files into the new file on the local PC.
3. Do not modify the original files in the supplied Network Path.
4. Select **File → Save As**.
5. Select **All Files** as the file type.
6. Change the file extension from `.txt` to `.sql`.
7. Save the consolidated deployment file using the required naming convention, for example:

   `Sql_Rep_Deploy.sql`

Repeat the same consolidation process for the Rollback file, if required.

### Important

Do not provide four separate files for Rep_Deploy and another four separate files for Rep_Rollback. The scripts must be consolidated according to the required naming convention.

## 5. Phase 1 Completion

This completes the folder creation and deployment package preparation process.

Before proceeding, verify that:

- The date-based folder follows the `DD-MMM-YYYY` format.
- The Server folder contains the required contents and excludes the prohibited items.
- The Register folder contains the Register and Unregister batch files.
- The Testing folder is included only when required.
- The Database folder contains the applicable Deploy and Rollback scripts.
- The files follow the required naming conventions.

articles.title: 02_Phase_2_VCDeploy_Client_and_Version_Configuration
articles.content:
# Auto-Deployment – Phase 2

## VCDeploy Client and Version Configuration

Use VCDeploy to create the Client and Client Version configuration and upload the prepared deployment package.

## 1. Sign In to VCDeploy

Open the VCDeploy sign-in page and sign in using the authorized account.

## 2. Create a New Client

Create a new Client in VCDeploy.

## 3. Verify the Client Name

After successfully creating the Client, verify that the Client Name is displayed in the Client List.

## 4. Open Client Version

From the sidebar, select:

1. **Client Version**
2. Click **Edit**.
3. Select the Client that was created.

## 5. Identify the Version Number

### 5.1 Open the Vici_Autodeployment Folder

Open the `Vici_Autodeployment` folder on `VTPL-079`.

### 5.2 Locate Reg_Key_path in the Config File

1. Open the `config` file.
2. Locate the `Reg_Key_path` value.
3. Open Registry Editor.
4. Navigate to the registry path specified by `Reg_Key_path`.

### 5.3 Check PreviousVersionInstalled

Check the value of `PreviousVersionInstalled` to identify the currently installed version.

#### Version Number Example

If the currently installed version is:

`9.1.1.2`

Enter the next version number in VCDeploy:

`9.1.1.3`

## 6. Upload the Prepared Deployment Package

Upload the ZIP file containing the four folders created during Phase 1 into VCDeploy.

Example ZIP filename from the procedure:

`30-Sep-2026.zip`

After uploading the package, click **Save Changes**.

## 7. Verify Deployment Readiness

After saving the changes, verify that the Client Version status is displayed as:

**Ready to Deploy**

### Important

Proceed to Phase 3 only after the status is confirmed as **Ready to Deploy**.

articles.title: 03_Phase_3_Server_Configuration_and_Execution
articles.content:
# Auto-Deployment – Phase 3

## Target Server Configuration and Deployment Execution

Proceed with Phase 3 only after the Client Version status in VCDeploy is confirmed as **Ready to Deploy**.

## 1. Take Remote Access of the Server

Use Remote Desktop Connection to access the target server.

The supplied procedure uses `VTPL-079` as the example server.

## 2. Navigate to the Vici_Autodeployment Folder

Navigate to:

`C:\Vici_Autodeployment`

Open the Auto-Deployment folder.

## 3. Configure config.json

Open the `config` file and navigate to the bottom of the configuration.

Configure the required Services and Task Scheduler entries in `config.json`.

### 3.1 Open the Services Window

1. Press `Win + R`.
2. Enter:

   `services.msc`

3. Press Enter to open the Services window.

### 3.2 Identify Relevant Service Names

Copy the names of the relevant services and enter them in the appropriate list in `config.json`.

Use the service names applicable to the target server.

### 3.3 Identify Relevant Task Scheduler Entries

1. Open Task Scheduler.
2. Identify tasks related to the `VTPL-079` server.
3. Check the task status.
4. Use task names whose status is **Ready**.

#### Important Notes

- Do not copy the names of tasks whose status is **Disabled**.
- If none of the tasks are in the Ready status, the supplied procedure instructs you to enable any one service and update it in the configuration file.

## 4. Execute Auto-Deployment Using Command Prompt

Open Command Prompt as an Administrator.

### 4.1 Change to the Vici_Autodeployment Folder

In Command Prompt, enter:

```cmd
cd <File path of Vici_Autodeployment folder>
```

Press Enter.

### 4.2 Execute the Deployment Command

Enter the following command:

```cmd
Deploy_main.exe vtpl-079
```

Press Enter.

#### Shortcut

Type `DEPLO` and press `TAB` to auto-fill `Deploy_main.exe`.

## 5. Auto-Deployment Execution

The Auto-Deployment process will start after the command is executed.

articles.title: 04_Failure_Handling_Rollback_and_Quick_Links
articles.content:
# Auto-Deployment – Failure Handling and References

## 1. Deployment Failure and Automatic Rollback

If the deployment fails, the system will automatically perform a rollback using the rollback scripts provided in the deployment package.

## 2. Retrying a Failed Deployment

If the deployment needs to be attempted again, follow these steps:

1. Make the necessary corrections based on the deployment failure.
2. Return to VCDeploy.
3. Refresh the Client Version page.
4. If required, upload the updated deployment package.
5. Click **Save Changes**.
6. Verify that the status is displayed as **Ready to Deploy**.
7. Proceed with the deployment again.

### Important

Proceed with another deployment attempt only after the required corrections have been made and the VCDeploy status is confirmed as **Ready to Deploy**.

## 3. Deployment Notification Emails

The source procedure contains examples of:

- Failed deployment notification email.
- Successful deployment notification email.

Review the relevant notification to understand whether the deployment attempt was unsuccessful or successful.

## 4. Quick Access Links

### Auto-Deployment Folder

```text
C:\Vici_Auto_deployment\ViciAutoDeployment
```

### Network Release Folder

```text
\\vtplsvr03\f\InternalRelease\ViciCloud 9.1.1.9\
```

### VCDeploy

Use the approved internal VCDeploy sign-in link.

## 5. Final Deployment Checklist

### Phase 1 – Package Preparation

- [ ] Date-based folder created using `DD-MMM-YYYY`.
- [ ] Server folder prepared and prohibited items excluded.
- [ ] Register and Unregister batch files included.
- [ ] Testing folder included if required.
- [ ] Applicable Database Deploy and Rollback scripts included.
- [ ] Required filenames verified.

### Phase 2 – VCDeploy Configuration

- [ ] New Client created.
- [ ] Client Name verified in the Client List.
- [ ] Correct Client selected under Client Version.
- [ ] Next version number identified using `PreviousVersionInstalled`.
- [ ] Prepared ZIP package uploaded.
- [ ] **Ready to Deploy** status confirmed.

### Phase 3 – Server Configuration and Execution

- [ ] Remote access to the target server established.
- [ ] Correct Vici_Autodeployment folder opened.
- [ ] Relevant service names configured in `config.json`.
- [ ] Relevant Ready Task Scheduler entries configured.
- [ ] Command Prompt opened as Administrator.
- [ ] Deployment command executed for the intended server.
- [ ] Deployment outcome reviewed.
- [ ] Rollback/retry procedure followed if deployment failed.

## 6. End of Procedure

This completes the documented ViciECM Auto-Deployment procedure.

articles.title: Basics of Deployment
articles.content:
# Basics of Deployment

## 1. Basics

### 1.1 What is Deployment?
- Applying changes to an existing application using Patch / Build Files is called Deployment.

### 1.2 What is Services Application?
- It is an application that displays a list of all the programs that actually run in the background.
- Press `Win + R` and type `services.msc` to open the Services window.

### 1.3 What is a Patch?
- A targeted fix of a bug can be called a Patch.

### 1.4 What is a Server and a Client?
- A computer providing services to other computers is called a Server.
- It receives requests from clients, processes those requests, and sends back a response.
- The Client's request is usually sent to the Application Server, which requests the necessary data from the Database Server.
- The Database Server sends the data to the Application Server, and the Application Server sends the data back to the Client.
- When accessing Google Chrome, the browser can act as a Client.
- An application requesting services from a server is called a Client.

### 1.5 What is an Environment?
- A setup where an application is installed and running for a particular purpose, with a particular version of the application.

#### Types of Environments
- DEV → Development
- QA → Testing
- UAT → User Acceptance
- PROD → Live / Production Use

---
## 2. Server Details

### 2.1 Deployment Server
- Server: VTPL-079
- Shared Path: `\\vtplsvr03\f\InternalRelease\ViciCloud 9.1.1.9`

articles.title: Manual Deployment Process
articles.content:
# VTPL-079 - Manual Deployment Process

## 1. Pre-Deployment Preparation

### 1.1 Locate the Update Files
- Navigate to the local PC's root directory where the application update files are provided.
- Navigate to the specified network path where the deployment-related files are stored.

### 1.2 Verify and Update Flags.ini
- Locate the `Server` folder and open `Flags.ini` using Notepad++.
- Before modifying the file, open Windows Registry Editor (`regedit`) and verify the existing application version number.
- Identify and note down the following:
  - Current Version Number: The version currently deployed.
  - Next Version Number: The version to which the application will be upgraded.
- Update the required version details in `Flags.ini` based on the registry information and deployment requirements.

## 2. Target Server and Patch Preparation

### 2.1 Access the Target Server
- Select the target server: `VTPL-079`.
- Access the VTPL-079 server.

### 2.2 Collect the Required Patch
- Locate and collect the required application patch file from the provided update location.
- Navigate to the directory containing the `Database` folder.
- Copy and paste the required application patch file into the same directory where the `Database` folder is located.

## 3. Create the Deployment Folder

### 3.1 Create a Date-Wise Folder
- On the local PC, navigate to:

C:\Vici-Updates\


- Create a new folder using the current deployment date.

Example:

C:\Vici-Updates\30-10-2026\

### 3.2 Copy the Database Folder
- Copy and paste the required `Database` folder into the newly created deployment folder.
- Verify that all required database scripts and deployment-related files are available before proceeding.

## 4. Stop IIS and Application Services

### 4.1 Stop IIS
- Open Command Prompt with Administrator privileges.
- Execute the following command:

cmd >iisreset -stop

### 4.2 Stop Application Services
- Stop the required application services on VTPL-079.
- If any service does not stop normally, identify the corresponding process through:

Task Manager > Details`

- Terminate the relevant process if required and authorized.

## 5. Backup and Patch Extraction

### 5.1 Execute the Deployment Package
- Execute the required patch deployment package.
- The deployment process will automatically initiate a backup.

### 5.2 Perform Incremental Backup
- Select the `Incremental Backup` option, if prompted.
- Verify that the backup process completes successfully.

### 5.3 Extract the Patch
- Once the backup is completed, allow the patch extraction process to continue.
- Ensure that the extraction process completes successfully.

## 6. Database Script Execution

### 6.1 Open SQL Server Management Studio
- Copy the extracted database scripts.
- Open SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS).

### 6.2 Execute Repository-Level Scripts
- Select the `VICIECMSS` database (Repository level).
- Open the SQL Query Editor.
- Copy and paste the required database scripts one after another.
- After pasting each script, click `Execute` to run it.
- Follow the prescribed execution order.

### 6.3 Execute RP-Level Scripts
- Select the `RpDOCmgr` database (RP level).
- Open the SQL Query Editor.
- Copy and paste the required database scripts one after another.
- After pasting each script, click `Execute` to run it.
- Follow the prescribed execution order.

### 6.4 Verify Script Execution
- Verify that each script executes successfully without errors.
- Proceed to the next script only after checking the execution result.
- Ensure that all required database scripts have been executed.

## 7. DCOM File Execution

### 7.1 Locate the DCOM File
- Locate the DCOM file provided with the deployment package.

### 7.2 Execute the DCOM File
- Execute the DCOM file as required by the deployment instructions.
- Verify that the execution completes successfully.

## 8. Application Configuration Changes

### 8.1 Review Configuration Instructions
- Review the `.txt` files provided with the patch.
- Identify the configuration changes specified in the respective text files.

### 8.2 Apply Configuration Changes
- Apply the required changes to the corresponding application configuration files and locations.
- Verify that the configuration values have been updated correctly.

## 9. Restart Application Services and IIS

### 9.1 Start Application Services
- Start all the required application services on VTPL-079.
- Verify that the services are running successfully.

### 9.2 Start IIS
- Open Command Prompt with Administrator privileges.
- Execute the following command:

cmd > iisreset -start

### 9.3 Verify IIS Status
- Confirm that IIS has started successfully.
- Ensure that all required application services are running.

## 10. Post-Deployment Verification

### 10.1 Application Verification
- Access the application and verify that it loads successfully.
- Confirm that the updated application version is reflected correctly.

### 10.2 Database Connectivity Verification
- Verify application connectivity with the database.
- Ensure that there are no database connectivity errors.

### 10.3 Functional Verification
- Perform basic application functionality checks.
- Verify that the application modules are accessible and functioning as expected.

### 10.4 Deployment Completion
- Confirm that all deployment activities have been completed successfully.
- Report any issues encountered during deployment to the concerned team.

articles.title: 00_Playwright_Installation_and_Configuration
articles.content:
# 00 – Installation and Environment Setup

## 1. Introduction

Before starting with Playwright automation, the development environment needs to be configured with the necessary tools, packages, and browser dependencies.

In this document, I have covered the installation and initial configuration of Python, Visual Studio Code, Playwright, Pytest, and the supporting libraries required to build and execute browser automation scripts.

The objective is to establish a working automation environment that can be used for developing, executing, and debugging automated test cases.

## 2. Prerequisites

The following tools and technologies are required for setting up the environment.

| Tool / Technology | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Python | Programming language used to develop automation scripts |
| Visual Studio Code | Code editor used for developing and managing the automation project |
| pip | Package installer used to install Python libraries |
| Playwright | Browser automation framework |
| Chromium / Firefox / WebKit | Browser engines used for executing automation scripts |
| Pytest | Framework used to organize and execute test cases |

## 3. Python Installation

Python is the primary programming language used for developing the Playwright automation framework.

### Installation Steps

1. Visit the official Python website.
2. Download the appropriate Python installer for Windows.
3. Run the downloaded installer.
4. Enable the **Add Python to PATH** option.
5. Proceed with the installation.
6. Once the installation is completed, open Command Prompt or the VS Code terminal.

**Website:** https://www.python.org/downloads/

### Verify Python Installation

Execute the following command:

```powershell
python --version
```

To verify the pip installation:

```powershell
pip --version
```

Both commands should return the installed version information.

## 4. Visual Studio Code Installation

Visual Studio Code is used as the primary development environment for writing, executing, and debugging Python automation scripts.

### Installation Steps

1. Visit the official Visual Studio Code website.
2. Download the Windows installer.
3. Run the installer and complete the installation.
4. Launch Visual Studio Code.

**Website:** https://code.visualstudio.com/

### Install Python Extension

After installing Visual Studio Code:

1. Open Visual Studio Code.
2. Navigate to the Extensions section.
3. Search for **Python**.
4. Install the Python extension published by Microsoft.

The Python extension provides Python language support, code execution, debugging, and interpreter selection.

## 5. Creating the Project Directory

Create a dedicated directory for the Playwright automation project.

For example:

```text
Playwright_Project/
│
├── Tests/
├── Locators/
├── Libraries/
├── Reports/
├── Screenshots/
├── Traces/
│
├── conftest.py
└── requirements.txt
```

This structure helps maintain the automation scripts, locators, reusable libraries, and execution reports separately.

Open the newly created project directory in Visual Studio Code.

## 6. Creating a Virtual Environment

A virtual environment provides an isolated Python environment for managing project-specific dependencies.

It helps avoid conflicts between packages installed for different Python projects.

Navigate to the project directory using the VS Code terminal.

Execute:

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
```

The above command creates a virtual environment named `.venv` inside the project directory.

### Activate the Virtual Environment

For Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

For Windows Command Prompt:

```cmd
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
```

Once activated, the environment name should appear at the beginning of the terminal prompt.

**Note:** Activate the virtual environment before installing project dependencies or executing automation scripts.

To deactivate the environment:

```powershell
deactivate
```

## 7. Upgrading pip

Before installing the required Python packages, upgrade pip to the latest available version.

Execute:

```powershell
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

This ensures that the package installer is updated before proceeding with the remaining installations.

## 8. Installing Playwright

Playwright is the primary browser automation framework used to interact with web applications.

It supports browser automation through Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

To install Playwright, execute:

```powershell
pip install playwright
```

Once the installation is completed, Playwright can be imported into Python scripts.

## 9. Installing Playwright Browsers

Installing the Playwright Python package and installing browser binaries are two separate steps.

Playwright requires compatible browser binaries to execute automation scripts. These binaries are downloaded separately using the Playwright CLI.

### 9.1 Install All Supported Browsers

Execute:

```powershell
python -m playwright install
```

This installs the default browser binaries supported by the installed Playwright version:

- Chromium
- Firefox
- WebKit

### 9.2 Install Individual Browsers

If only a specific browser is required, it can be installed independently.

**Chromium**

```powershell
python -m playwright install chromium
```

**Firefox**

```powershell
python -m playwright install firefox
```

**WebKit**

```powershell
python -m playwright install webkit
```

### 9.3 Verify Browser Installation

To view the browser installations managed by Playwright, execute:

```powershell
python -m playwright install --list
```

### Important Notes

- Playwright downloads browser versions compatible with the installed Playwright package.
- Browser binaries are stored separately from the Python project.
- Updating Playwright may require installing the corresponding browser binaries again.
- Browser installation requires an internet connection.

## 10. Installing Pytest

Pytest is the testing framework used to organize, execute, and manage automation test cases.

It provides features such as test discovery, fixtures, assertions, parameterization, and execution reporting.

Install Pytest using:

```powershell
pip install pytest
```

Verify the installation:

```powershell
pytest --version
```

## 11. Installing pytest-playwright

The `pytest-playwright` package provides integration between Playwright and Pytest.

It provides ready-to-use fixtures such as:

- `page`
- `context`
- `browser`
- `browser_type`

It also supports browser selection and other Playwright-specific command-line options during test execution.

Install the package:

```powershell
pip install pytest-playwright
```

**Note:** This package is useful when using the official Playwright Pytest fixtures. It is not mandatory when implementing browser management and fixtures entirely through the Playwright Python library.

## 12. Installing Supporting Python Libraries

Apart from Playwright and Pytest, additional Python libraries can be installed to support reporting, Excel operations, clipboard interactions, and image processing.

### 12.1 pytest-html

```powershell
pip install pytest-html
```

Used to generate HTML test execution reports.

### 12.2 allure-pytest

```powershell
pip install allure-pytest
```

Provides Allure integration with Pytest for collecting test execution results.

### 12.3 openpyxl

```powershell
pip install openpyxl
```

Used to read, write, and manipulate Excel workbooks.

### 12.4 pyperclip

```powershell
pip install pyperclip
```

Used to interact with the system clipboard, including copying and retrieving text.

### 12.5 Pillow

```powershell
pip install pillow
```

Used for image processing, opening images, and performing image-related operations.

### Installation Summary

The supporting libraries can also be installed together:

```powershell
pip install pytest-html allure-pytest openpyxl pyperclip pillow
```

## 13. Configuring the Python Interpreter in VS Code

After creating the virtual environment, configure Visual Studio Code to use the Python interpreter associated with the project.

### Steps

1. Open the Playwright project in Visual Studio Code.
2. Press `Ctrl + Shift + P`.
3. Search for `Python: Select Interpreter`.
4. Select the interpreter located inside the project's `.venv` directory.
5. Open a new terminal.
6. Verify that the virtual environment is activated.

This ensures that the project uses the correct Python interpreter and the packages installed within its virtual environment.

## 14. Managing Project Dependencies

Once all the required packages have been installed, create a `requirements.txt` file.

This file maintains a record of the installed Python packages and their versions.

Execute:

```powershell
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

To install the same dependencies in another environment:

```powershell
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Maintaining this file helps reproduce the Python environment without manually installing each package.

**Important:** `requirements.txt` records Python package dependencies. It does not install Playwright browser binaries. Browser installation must be performed separately.

## 15. Verifying the Complete Installation

After completing the installation and configuration, verify that all the required tools and packages are available.

Execute the following commands individually.

**Python**

```powershell
python --version
```

**pip**

```powershell
pip --version
```

**Playwright**

```powershell
python -m playwright --version
```

**Pytest**

```powershell
pytest --version
```

**Installed Python Packages**

```powershell
pip list
```

**Playwright Browser Installation**

```powershell
python -m playwright install --list
```

If the commands execute successfully and the required browser binaries are available, the installation can proceed to the first automation test.

## 16. Creating and Executing the First Automation Test

To verify that Playwright and Pytest are working together, create a Python file named `test_example.py` inside the `Tests` directory.

Add the following code:

```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

def test_open_website():

    with sync_playwright() as p:

        browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=False)

        page = browser.new_page()

        page.goto("https://playwright.dev/")

        print(page.title())

        browser.close()
```

### Execute the Test

Navigate to the project root directory and execute:

```powershell
python -m pytest Tests/test_example.py -v -s
```

### Expected Result

1. Playwright launches the Chromium browser.
2. The browser navigates to the Playwright official website.
3. The page title is retrieved and displayed in the terminal.
4. The browser closes after execution.
5. Pytest displays the test execution result.

If the test passes, it confirms that the basic Python, Playwright, Chromium, and Pytest setup is working.

## 17. Common Installation and Configuration Issues

| Issue | Possible Resolution |
|---|---|
| Python command not recognized | Verify Python installation and PATH configuration |
| pip command not recognized | Verify pip installation and use `python -m pip` |
| Playwright browser executable not found | Execute `python -m playwright install` |
| ModuleNotFoundError | Verify the selected Python interpreter and install the missing package |
| Virtual environment activation failure | Verify the activation command for the selected terminal |
| Pytest does not discover test cases | Verify test file names and function names |
| Browser installation failure | Check internet connectivity, proxy restrictions, and download permissions |
| Playwright browser version mismatch | Update the browser binaries using the Playwright installation command |

## 18. Important Commands Reference

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `python --version` | Checks the Python version |
| `pip --version` | Checks the pip version |
| `python -m venv .venv` | Creates a virtual environment |
| `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` | Activates the virtual environment in PowerShell |
| `deactivate` | Deactivates the virtual environment |
| `python -m pip install --upgrade pip` | Upgrades pip |
| `pip install playwright` | Installs Playwright |
| `python -m playwright install` | Installs Playwright browser binaries |
| `python -m playwright install chromium` | Installs Chromium |
| `python -m playwright install --list` | Lists Playwright browser installations |
| `pip install pytest` | Installs Pytest |
| `pip install pytest-playwright` | Installs Playwright's Pytest integration |
| `pip list` | Lists installed Python packages |
| `pip freeze` | Lists installed packages with versions |
| `pip freeze > requirements.txt` | Saves package versions into requirements.txt |
| `pip install -r requirements.txt` | Installs packages from requirements.txt |
| `python -m pytest` | Executes Pytest |

## 19. Conclusion

With the installation and configuration steps completed, the development environment is ready for Playwright automation using Python and Pytest.

The next step is to understand Playwright, its architecture, important features, and how it interacts with web applications.

This provides the foundation for developing structured, reusable, and maintainable automation scripts.

articles.title: 01_Introduction_to_Playwright
articles.content:
# Introduction to Playwright

## 1. Introduction to Playwright

### 1.1 What is Playwright?

Playwright is an open-source browser automation and end-to-end testing framework developed by Microsoft.

It allows developers and testers to automate browser interactions programmatically using languages such as Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java and .NET.

Playwright can interact with web applications just like a real user by navigating between pages, clicking buttons, entering text, selecting options, uploading files and validating application behaviour.

It supports three major browser engines:

- **Chromium** – Used by browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge.
- **Firefox** – Mozilla Firefox browser engine.
- **WebKit** – Browser engine used by Safari.

### 1.2 What is Browser Automation?

Browser automation is the process of controlling a web browser programmatically to perform actions that would otherwise require manual interaction.

Instead of manually opening a website, entering credentials, navigating through pages and checking results, an automation script performs these activities automatically.

#### 1.2.1 Common Browser Automation Activities

- Opening and navigating to websites.
- Clicking buttons, links and other interactive elements.
- Entering text into input fields.
- Selecting options from dropdown menus.
- Checking and unchecking checkboxes.
- Submitting forms.
- Validating text, messages and application elements.
- Uploading and downloading files.
- Handling browser tabs, windows, frames and dialogs.
- Capturing screenshots and recording test traces.

#### 1.2.2 What Can Playwright Automate?

Playwright is primarily designed for browser automation, but it also provides capabilities for API testing, network handling and mobile browser emulation.

**1. Web Browsers**

- Chromium-based browsers.
- Mozilla Firefox.
- WebKit-based browsers.

**2. Web Applications**

- Login and authentication workflows.
- Dashboards and reports.
- Forms and data-entry operations.
- Tables, grids and pagination.
- Menus, dropdowns and navigation.
- Document management systems.
- CRM, ERP and other browser-based business applications.

**3. User Interactions**

- Mouse clicks and double-clicks.
- Keyboard input and keyboard shortcuts.
- Text entry and selection.
- Drag-and-drop operations.
- Hover interactions.
- Checkbox and radio-button operations.

**4. Forms and Data Validation**

- Filling and submitting forms.
- Validating mandatory fields.
- Checking validation messages.
- Verifying entered and displayed data.
- Testing dropdowns and multi-select controls.

**5. File Operations**

- Uploading files.
- Downloading files.
- Validating downloaded files.
- Handling file chooser dialogs.
- Working with file contents through Python.

**6. Browser Windows, Tabs and Frames**

- Handling multiple browser tabs.
- Switching between pages.
- Managing pop-up windows.
- Interacting with iframes.
- Handling JavaScript alerts, confirmations and prompts.

**7. API Testing**

Playwright provides `APIRequestContext` to send HTTP requests and validate API responses independently of browser interactions.

Common operations include:

- GET
- POST
- PUT
- PATCH
- DELETE

**8. Network Operations**

- Monitoring network requests and responses.
- Intercepting browser requests.
- Mocking API responses.
- Modifying request and response behaviour.
- Validating network activity.

**9. Mobile Browser Testing**

Playwright supports mobile device emulation, including:

- Mobile screen dimensions.
- Device scale factor.
- Touch input.
- Mobile browser behaviour.
- Device-specific browser configurations.

**10. Testing and Diagnostic Operations**

- Capturing screenshots.
- Recording videos.
- Generating execution traces.
- Inspecting test failures.
- Debugging browser interactions.
- Validating page content and application behaviour.

**Important Limitation**

Playwright is not a general-purpose desktop or native mobile automation framework. It does not directly automate native Windows desktop applications or native Android and iOS applications through their native interfaces.

It can, however, automate websites and web applications accessed through mobile browsers using device emulation.

#### 1.2.3 Example: Basic Browser Automation

The following example demonstrates how Playwright opens a browser, navigates to a website, retrieves the page title and closes the browser.

```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:

    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=False)

    page = browser.new_page()

    page.goto("https://www.google.com")

    print(page.title())

    browser.close()
```

**Code Explanation**

| Code | Description |
|---|---|
| `sync_playwright()` | Initializes the synchronous Playwright API. |
| `p.chromium.launch()` | Launches a Chromium browser instance. |
| `headless=False` | Opens the browser in visible mode. |
| `browser.new_page()` | Creates a new page using a new browser context. |
| `page.goto()` | Navigates to the specified URL. |
| `page.title()` | Retrieves the current page title. |
| `browser.close()` | Closes the browser instance. |

### 2. Features of Playwright

**1. Cross-Browser Support**

Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, allowing tests to run across different browser engines.

**2. Auto-Waiting**

Playwright automatically waits for elements to satisfy the necessary actionability conditions before performing actions such as clicking.

**3. Web-First Assertions**

Playwright provides assertions that automatically retry until the expected condition is satisfied or the timeout is reached.

**4. Multiple Browser Contexts**

Browser contexts allow independent browser sessions within the same browser instance.

**5. Parallel Test Execution**

Playwright can execute tests in parallel when integrated with suitable test runners such as pytest.

**6. Network Interception**

Playwright can monitor, intercept and modify network requests and responses.

**7. Screenshots and Video Recording**

Playwright supports capturing screenshots and recording videos for debugging and reporting.

**8. Trace Viewer**

Playwright provides a Trace Viewer to inspect test execution, actions, DOM snapshots, network activity and other debugging information.

**9. Headless and Headed Execution**

- Headless mode: Executes the browser without displaying its graphical interface.
- Headed mode: Executes the browser with its graphical interface visible.

**10. Synchronous and Asynchronous APIs**

Playwright for Python provides both synchronous and asynchronous APIs.

### 3. Playwright and pytest

Playwright is a browser automation library, whereas pytest is a Python testing framework.

They serve different purposes and can be integrated to build automated testing frameworks.

| Playwright | pytest |
|---|---|
| Automates browser interactions. | Executes and manages test cases. |
| Provides browser automation APIs. | Provides test discovery and execution. |
| Interacts with web elements. | Provides fixtures and test setup. |
| Supports browser assertions. | Provides test organization and reporting integrations. |
| Handles browser operations. | Manages test execution and results. |

**Why Use Playwright with pytest?**

- Organizing test cases into separate files.
- Reusing browser setup through fixtures.
- Managing test execution.
- Supporting parametrized tests.
- Running tests in parallel using plugins.
- Generating test reports through reporting plugins.

### 4. Basic Playwright Test Using pytest

**Example:**

```python
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_homepage(page: Page):

    page.goto("https://www.google.com")

    expect(page).to_have_title("Google")
```

**Code Explanation**

| Code | Description |
|---|---|
| `Page` | Type annotation representing a Playwright page. |
| `expect` | Provides Playwright assertions. |
| `test_homepage()` | A pytest test function. |
| `page` | Browser page fixture provided by the pytest-playwright plugin. |
| `page.goto()` | Navigates to the specified website. |
| `expect(page).to_have_title()` | Validates the page title. |

**Execution Command:**

```bash
python -m pytest test_playwright_intro.py
```

The `pytest-playwright` plugin provides fixtures such as `page`, `context` and `browser` for use in pytest test cases.

### 5. Important Playwright Objects

| Object | Description |
|---|---|
| Playwright | Entry point for accessing Playwright browser automation functionality. |
| BrowserType | Represents a browser engine such as Chromium, Firefox or WebKit. |
| Browser | Represents a launched browser instance. |
| BrowserContext | Represents an isolated browser session. |
| Page | Represents an individual browser tab or page. |
| Locator | Represents a way to find and interact with DOM elements. |
| Frame | Represents a frame within a page. |
| Download | Represents a file download. |
| Request | Represents a network request. |
| Response | Represents a network response. |

### 6. Playwright Automation Workflow

A typical browser automation workflow follows these steps:

1. Initialize Playwright.
2. Launch the required browser.
3. Create a browser context.
4. Open a new page.
5. Navigate to the application.
6. Locate web elements.
7. Perform user interactions.
8. Validate expected results.
9. Capture debugging information when required.
10. Close the browser.

### 7. Common Use Cases of Playwright

- Web application functional testing.
- End-to-end testing.
- Regression testing.
- Cross-browser testing.
- UI testing.
- API testing.
- Network testing.
- Form validation.
- File upload and download testing.
- Authentication and session testing.
- Automated browser workflows.

### 8. Official References

**Playwright Documentation**

https://playwright.dev/python/docs/intro

**Playwright Python API Reference**

https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-playwright

**Page API**

https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api/class-page

**Network Documentation**

https://playwright.dev/python/docs/network

**API Testing**

https://playwright.dev/python/docs/api-testing

**pytest Documentation**

https://docs.pytest.org/

articles.content:
# Playwright with Python – Locators and Selectors ## 1. Introduction to Locators ### What is a Locator? A locator is a mechanism provided by Playwright to identify elements on a web page so that automated tests can interact with them or verify their state. For example, when automating a login page, we need to identify: - Username input field. - Password input field. - Login button. - Error or success messages. Playwright provides several built-in locator methods to identify these elements based on how users perceive and interact with the application. These include: - Role - Label - Placeholder - Visible text - Alternative text - Title - Test ID ### What is a Selector? A selector is a way of specifying which element or elements Playwright should identify on a web page. In simple terms, it defines the criteria used to locate an element. Playwright provides different ways to identify elements, including user-facing locator methods and other selector strategies. ### How Playwright Locators Work A locator does not permanently store a reference to a DOM element. Playwright resolves the locator against the current page when an action or assertion is performed. This helps locators work with dynamically updated web pages. ### Basic Example **HTML:** ```html
``` **Playwright Python:** ```python from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright with sync_playwright() as p: browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=False) page = browser.new_page() page.goto("https://example.com") page.get_by_label("Username").fill("admin") page.get_by_label("Password").fill("password123") page.get_by_role("button", name="Login").click() browser.close() ``` ### Explanation - `page` represents the browser tab. - `get_by_label()` identifies the input fields through their associated labels. - `get_by_role()` identifies the Login button using its role and accessible name. - `fill()` enters text into an input field. - `click()` performs the button interaction. - `browser.close()` closes the browser. ## 2. Types of Locators in Playwright | **Locator** | **Purpose** | |---|---| | `get_by_role()` | Identifies elements by their role and accessible name. | | `get_by_label()` | Identifies form controls through associated labels. | | `get_by_placeholder()` | Identifies input fields using placeholder text. | | `get_by_text()` | Identifies elements using visible text. | | `get_by_alt_text()` | Identifies elements using alternative text. | | `get_by_title()` | Identifies elements using their title attribute. | | `get_by_test_id()` | Identifies elements using a test ID. | | `locator()` | Identifies elements using CSS or XPath selectors. | --- ## 3. User-Facing Locators ### 3.1 get_by_role() `get_by_role()` identifies an element using its ARIA role and accessible name. **Syntax:** ```python page.get_by_role("role", name="accessible name") ``` **Example 1 – Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role("button", name="Save").click() ``` **Example 2 – Link** HTML: ```html Dashboard ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role("link", name="Dashboard").click() ``` **Example 3 – Checkbox** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role( "checkbox", name="Remember me" ).check() ``` **Example 4 – Radio Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role( "radio", name="Male" ).check() ``` **Example 5 – Heading** HTML: ```html

Dashboard

``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role( "heading", name="Dashboard" ).is_visible() ``` **Example 6 – Table Row** HTML: ```html
Invoice_001.pdf Approved
``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role( "row", name="Invoice_001.pdf Approved" ).is_visible() ``` **Example 7 – Dropdown** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_label("Department").select_option( label="Engineering" ) ``` **Common ARIA roles:** | Role | HTML example | |---|---| | `button` | ` ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_text( "Save", exact=True ).click() ``` **Example 3 – Partial Text Matching** HTML: ```html
Document uploaded successfully. File ID: 1025
``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_text( "Document uploaded successfully" ).is_visible() ``` **Example 4 – Error Message** HTML: ```html Invalid username or password ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_text( "Invalid username or password" ).is_visible() ``` **Example 5 – Menu Item** HTML: ```html
Settings
``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_text( "Settings", exact=True ).click() ``` **Important:** For buttons and links, prefer `get_by_role()` when their role and accessible name are available. ### 3.5 get_by_alt_text() `get_by_alt_text()` identifies elements using their alternative text, generally an image's `alt` attribute. **Example 1 – Company Logo** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_alt_text( "Company Logo" ).is_visible() ``` **Example 2 – Profile Image** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_alt_text( "User Profile" ).is_visible() ``` ### 3.6 get_by_title() `get_by_title()` identifies an element through its HTML `title` attribute. **Example 1 – Refresh Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_title( "Refresh Documents" ).click() ``` **Example 2 – Delete Icon** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_title( "Delete Document" ).click() ``` ### 3.7 get_by_test_id() `get_by_test_id()` identifies elements using a dedicated test ID attribute. **Example 1 – Save Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_test_id( "save-document" ).click() ``` **Example 2 – Document Name** HTML: ```html
Invoice_001.pdf
``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_test_id( "document-name" ).is_visible() ``` **Example 3 – Search Input** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_test_id( "document-search" ).fill("Invoice") ``` **Important:** Test IDs are intended for automated testing. They are generally more stable than selectors based on styling classes. ---

articles.title: 03_CSS_Selectors_And_Xpath
articles.content:
## 4. CSS Selectors CSS selectors identify elements using HTML tags, IDs, classes, attributes and relationships. In Playwright Python: ```python page.locator("CSS_SELECTOR") ``` ### 4.1 Locate by ID An ID selector uses `#` followed by the element's ID. **Example 1 – Username** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("#username").fill("admin") ``` **Example 2 – Login Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("#loginBtn").click() ``` **Example 3 – Search Field** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("#searchBox").fill("Invoice") ``` ### 4.2 Locate by Class A class selector uses `.` followed by the class name. **Example 1 – Save Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator(".save-button").click() ``` **Example 2 – Multiple Classes** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( ".btn.primary.save-button" ).click() ``` **Example 3 – Input Field** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( ".form-control" ).fill("admin") ``` ### 4.3 Locate by Tag Name A tag selector identifies elements using their HTML tag. **Example 1 – Button** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("button").count() ``` **Example 2 – Input** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("input").count() ``` **Example 3 – Table** HTML: ```html
Invoice.pdf
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("table").count() ``` ### 4.4 Locate by Attribute Attribute selectors identify elements using their HTML attributes. **Example 1 – Name Attribute** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( 'input[name="username"]' ).fill("admin") ``` **Example 2 – Type Attribute** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( 'input[type="password"]' ).fill("password123") ``` **Example 3 – Placeholder Attribute** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '[placeholder="Search Documents"]' ).fill("Invoice") ``` **Example 4 – Data Attribute** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '[data-action="delete"]' ).click() ``` **Example 5 – Partial Attribute Matching** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( 'input[name^="user"]' ) ``` CSS attribute operators: | Operator | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | `=` | Exact match | `[type="text"]` | | `^=` | Starts with | `[name^="user"]` | | `$=` | Ends with | `[name$="email"]` | | `*=` | Contains | `[name*="user"]` | | `~=` | Contains a whitespace-separated word | `[class~="active"]` | | `|=` | Exact value or value followed by a hyphen | `[lang|="en"]` | ### 4.5 Combining CSS Selectors Multiple selectors can be combined to narrow down the target. **Example 1 – Tag and ID** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("input#username") ``` **Example 2 – Tag and Class** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("button.save-button") ``` **Example 3 – Tag and Attribute** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( 'input[type="text"][name="username"]' ) ``` **Example 4 – Parent and Child** HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( ".login-form input" ).fill("admin") ``` **Example 5 – Direct Child** HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( ".login-form > input" ).fill("admin") ``` The space selector matches descendants at any depth. The `>` selector matches only direct children. ### 4.6 CSS Pseudo-Classes CSS pseudo-classes allow elements to be identified based on their position or state. **Example 1 – First Child** HTML: ```html
  • Administration
  • Users
  • Groups
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( "ul li:first-child" ).click() ``` **Example 2 – Last Child** Playwright: ```python page.locator( "ul li:last-child" ).click() ``` **Example 3 – Nth Child** Playwright: ```python page.locator( "ul li:nth-child(2)" ).click() ``` **Example 4 – Checked Checkbox** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( 'input[type="checkbox"]:checked' ).count() ``` **Example 5 – Enabled Input** HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( "input:enabled" ).count() ``` --- ## 5. XPath Locators XPath is a query language used to navigate and identify elements in an HTML or XML document. XPath can identify elements using tags, attributes, text, parent-child relationships, ancestors and siblings. In Playwright Python: ```python page.locator("xpath=EXPRESSION") ``` Playwright also recognises XPath expressions passed directly to `locator()` when they begin with `//` or `..`. ### 5.1 XPath Using Tag Name HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("//button").count() ``` ### 5.2 XPath Using ID HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//*[@id="username"]' ).fill("admin") ``` ### 5.3 XPath Using Class HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//button[@class="save-button"]' ).click() ``` For multiple class names, use a class-token expression: HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//button[contains(concat(" ", normalize-space(@class), " "), " save-button ")]' ).click() ``` ### 5.4 XPath Using Text HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//button[text()="Save Document"]' ).click() ``` Partial text: ```python page.locator( '//button[contains(text(), "Save")]' ).click() ``` Text with surrounding whitespace: ```python page.locator( '//button[normalize-space(.)="Save Document"]' ).click() ``` ### 5.5 XPath Using Multiple Attributes HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//input[@type="text" and @name="username"]' ).fill("admin") ``` Another example: HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//button[@type="button" and @title="Refresh Documents"]' ).click() ``` ### 5.6 XPath Using Parent and Child Relationships HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//div[@class="login-form"]//input[@name="username"]' ).fill("admin") ``` Direct child: ```python page.locator( '//div[@class="login-form"]/input[@name="username"]' ).fill("admin") ``` Difference: - `/` selects a direct child. - `//` selects a descendant at any depth. ### 5.7 XPath Using Parent Axis HTML: ```html
Invoice_001.pdf
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//span[text()="Invoice_001.pdf"]/parent::div' ).is_visible() ``` ### 5.8 XPath Using Ancestor Axis HTML: ```html
Invoice_001.pdf
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//span[text()="Invoice_001.pdf"]/ancestor::div[@class="document-container"]' ).is_visible() ``` ### 5.9 XPath Using Following-Sibling HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//label[text()="Username"]/following-sibling::input' ).fill("admin") ``` ### 5.10 XPath Using Preceding-Sibling HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '//label[text()="Username"]/preceding-sibling::input' ).fill("admin") ``` ### 5.11 XPath Using Position HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python page.locator( '(//div[@class="documents"]/button)[1]' ).click() ``` XPath positions start at 1, unlike Playwright's `nth()`, which starts at 0. ### 5.12 XPath Axes Reference | Axis | Purpose | |---|---| | `parent::` | Selects the parent | | `child::` | Selects direct children | | `ancestor::` | Selects ancestors | | `descendant::` | Selects descendants | | `following-sibling::` | Selects following siblings | | `preceding-sibling::` | Selects preceding siblings | | `following::` | Selects nodes that follow the current node | | `preceding::` | Selects nodes that precede the current node | ---

articles.title: 04_Advanced_Locator_Strategies
articles.content:
## 6. Advanced Locator Techniques ### 6.1 Chaining Locators Chaining narrows down a search by locating an element inside another locator. HTML: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python login_form = page.locator(".login-form") login_form.locator( 'input[name="username"]' ).fill("admin") login_form.locator( 'input[name="password"]' ).fill("password123") login_form.get_by_role( "button", name="Login" ).click() ``` The search is restricted to the login form instead of matching inputs across the entire page. ### 6.2 filter() `filter()` narrows down an existing locator using text or another locator. HTML: ```html
Invoice_001.pdf
Invoice_002.pdf
Invoice_003.pdf
``` Playwright: ```python document = page.locator( ".document-row" ).filter( has_text="Invoice_002.pdf" ) document.get_by_role( "button", name="Download" ).click() ``` **Using has:** HTML: ```html

Invoice_001.pdf

Invoice_002.pdf

``` Playwright: ```python document = page.locator( ".document-row" ).filter( has=page.get_by_role( "heading", name="Invoice_002.pdf" ) ) document.get_by_role( "button", name="Download" ).click() ``` **Using has_not:** ```python document = page.locator( ".document-row" ).filter( has_not=page.get_by_text("Deleted") ) ``` This example excludes rows containing the text `Deleted`. ### 6.3 first Selects the first matching element. HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_role( "button", name="Edit" ).first.click() ``` ### 6.4 last Selects the last matching element. ```python page.get_by_role( "button", name="Edit" ).last.click() ``` ### 6.5 nth() Selects an element using its zero-based position. HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python page.locator("button").nth(0).click() page.locator("button").nth(1).click() page.locator("button").nth(2).click() ``` | Index | Element | |---|---| | `nth(0)` | First element | | `nth(1)` | Second element | | `nth(2)` | Third element | **Important:** Use positional selection only when the ordering is known and stable. A change in sorting or page layout can change which element an index identifies. ### 6.6 and_() `and_()` combines two locators. The resulting locator matches elements that satisfy both conditions. HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python button = page.get_by_role( "button" ).and_( page.get_by_title("Save Document") ) button.click() ``` ### 6.7 or_() `or_()` combines alternative locators. HTML: ```html
``` Alternative page state: ```html
``` Playwright: ```python continue_button = page.get_by_role( "button", name="Continue" ) login_button = page.get_by_role( "button", name="Sign In" ) alternative_button = continue_button.or_( login_button ) alternative_button.first.click() ``` **Important:** If both elements are present, the combined locator can match multiple elements. Check the current page state before interacting with it. --- ## 7. Handling Multiple Matching Elements One common issue in automation is when a locator identifies more than one element. HTML: ```html
Invoice_001.pdf
Invoice_002.pdf
Invoice_003.pdf
``` Incorrect implementation: ```python page.locator("#chkSelect").check() ``` This locator matches multiple checkboxes. ### Step 1 – Count matching elements ```python checkboxes = page.locator("#chkSelect") print(checkboxes.count()) ``` ### Step 2 – Identify the required row ```python document_row = page.get_by_role( "row" ).filter( has_text="Invoice_002.pdf" ) ``` ### Step 3 – Locate the checkbox inside that row ```python document_row.locator( "#chkSelect" ).check() ``` **Important:** Repeated IDs are invalid HTML. A better application implementation would use a class or a unique identifier for each checkbox. Scoping the locator can work around the issue, but it does not fix the underlying HTML defect. --- ## 8. Strict Mode Violations Playwright applies strictness to operations that require a single element. If a locator matches multiple elements, an action such as `click()` can raise a strict-mode violation. HTML: ```html
Please wait for a short while
Please wait for a short while
``` Playwright: ```python page.get_by_text( "Please wait for a short while" ).click() ``` This can fail because two elements match. ### Step 1 – Count the matches ```python message = page.get_by_text( "Please wait for a short while" ) print(message.count()) ``` ### Step 2 – Inspect the matching elements ```python for index in range(message.count()): print( index, message.nth(index).text_content() ) ``` ### Step 3 – Identify the correct element Use a parent container, a unique attribute, a role or another condition to narrow down the locator. ### Step 4 – Perform the action ```python message.first.click() ``` Only use `.first` after verifying that the first element is actually the intended target. **Remember:** `count()` helps diagnose multiple matches. It does not automatically guarantee that the page will remain unchanged between counting and interacting. ---

## 9. Working with Iframes An iframe embeds another HTML document inside the current page. HTML: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python document_frame = page.frame_locator( "#documentFrame" ) document_frame.get_by_role( "button", name="Download" ).click() ``` ### 9.1 CSS Inside an Iframe HTML inside the iframe: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python document_frame.locator( "#chkSelect" ).check() ``` ### 9.2 Role Locator Inside an Iframe HTML inside the iframe: ```html ``` Playwright: ```python document_frame.get_by_role( "button", name="Download" ).click() ``` ### 9.3 Text Locator Inside an Iframe HTML inside the iframe: ```html
Document loaded successfully
``` Playwright: ```python document_frame.get_by_text( "Document loaded successfully" ).is_visible() ``` ### 9.4 Practical ECM Example ```python IF_DOC_IFRAME = page.frame_locator( "iframe" ) IF_DOC_IFRAME.locator( "#chkSelect" ).check() ``` Replace the iframe selector with the actual unique iframe locator in your application. For applications containing multiple iframes, identify the correct iframe before interacting with its contents. --- ## 10. Locator Methods and Useful Operations | Method / Property | Purpose | |---|---| | `count()` | Returns the number of matching elements | | `first` | Selects the first matching element | | `last` | Selects the last matching element | | `nth(index)` | Selects an element by zero-based position | | `click()` | Click

articles.title: 06_Codegen
articles.content:
# Playwright with Python – Codegen

## 1. Introduction to Codegen

### What is Codegen?

Codegen (Code Generator) is a built-in Playwright tool that automatically generates automation code based on user interactions with a web application.

It records actions performed in a browser, such as:

- Clicking buttons.
- Entering text into input fields.
- Selecting dropdown options.
- Navigating between pages.
- Interacting with other web elements.

Codegen generates the corresponding Playwright code, helping testers create automation scripts without manually writing every interaction.

### 1.1 Advantages of Codegen

- Automatically generates Playwright code.
- Helps identify suitable locators.
- Reduces manual coding effort.
- Useful for learning Playwright syntax.
- Helps quickly create initial automation scripts.
- Supports generating code in Python and other supported languages.

## 2. Launching Codegen

Playwright Codegen can be launched directly from the terminal.

### 2.1 Basic Command

```bash
playwright codegen
```

This opens a browser window and the Playwright Inspector.

### 2.2 Launch Codegen with a URL

```bash
python -m playwright codegen https://example.com
```

This opens the specified website directly in the browser.

## 3. Understanding the Codegen Interface

When Codegen starts, two main windows are displayed:

### 3.1 Browser Window

The browser window allows you to interact with the application.

You can perform actions such as:

- Clicking buttons.
- Filling input fields.
- Selecting options.
- Navigating through application pages.

Codegen records these interactions and generates the corresponding automation code.

### 3.2 Playwright Inspector

The Playwright Inspector displays the generated Playwright code.

It also provides locator suggestions when interacting with elements.

You can inspect the generated code and use it as a starting point for your automation scripts.

## 4. Official Documentation

[Playwright – Test Generator](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/codegen)
